topic: Assessing the Sick and Deteriorating Child
parentTitle: Assessing the Sick and Deteriorating Child
title: Dehydration, oral rehydration and IV fluids in children
blurb: Recognise dehydration and shock in a child, plan oral rehydration, and calculate and monitor IV maintenance fluids safely using NICE CG84 and NG29.
question: Lily, 2, weighs 14 kg and has clinical dehydration from gastroenteritis without shock. Oral rehydration solution is prescribed. How much should she receive over the next 4 hours, in addition to maintenance?

teach.body: Children have a higher body water content and a higher metabolic rate than adults, so they lose fluid quickly with vomiting, diarrhoea or fever. Formally, clinical dehydration is a deficit of body water with signs such as dry mucous membranes, reduced urine output and tachycardia; clinical shock is circulatory failure with poor perfusion. Plain English: watch for a quiet, dry child passing little urine, and act before they become cold and mottled.

teach.caption: Red flags for dehydration: appears unwell, altered responsiveness, sunken eyes, tachycardia, tachypnoea, reduced skin turgor.

steps.label: No dehydration
steps.sub: Continue breastfeeds and usual fluids; 5 mL/kg ORS after each large watery stool if at risk

steps.label: Clinical dehydration
steps.sub: Low-osmolarity ORS 50 mL/kg over 4 h plus maintenance, small and often

teach.caption: Avoid fruit juices and fizzy drinks. If shock persists after a second bolus, consider intensive care.

head: Body weight
Fluid per day
teach.caption: Males rarely need more than 2,500 mL/day and females 2,000 mL/day. Example: 16 kg = 1,000 + 300 = 1,300 mL/day (about 54 mL/h).

teach.body: Initial IV maintenance fluid is an isotonic crystalloid with sodium 131 to 154 mmol/L, with glucose added as needed. Measure plasma electrolytes and glucose when starting IV fluids and at least every 24 hours, and weigh the child daily. Keep an accurate fluid balance chart. Restrict to 50 to 80% of maintenance if there is a risk of fluid overload, for example with raised antidiuretic hormone (ADH) secretion.

items.label: rapid bolus for shock, then reassess

teach.caption: Hypernatraemic dehydration: replace the deficit slowly over 48 hours, aiming for a sodium fall under 0.5 mmol/L per hour.

teach.text: Hypotonic fluids such as 0.18% sodium chloride with 4% glucose are not the initial maintenance fluid: they risk hyponatraemia and cerebral oedema. NG29 starts with an isotonic crystalloid (sodium 131 to 154 mmol/L).

teach.h: Scenario: Noah, 18 months, in the assessment unit
teach.body: Noah weighs 11 kg and has had gastroenteritis for 3 days. He is pale, mottled and cold with a CRT of 5 seconds. Nurse Priya recognises shock and calls for help. A 110 mL (10 mL/kg) bolus of 0.9% sodium chloride is given rapidly and Noah is reassessed. Once perfusion improves, his deficit is calculated at 100 mL/kg plus maintenance, and Priya starts strict fluid balance, daily weights and checks electrolytes and glucose.

items: Keep breastfeeding and offer usual fluids; give ORS small and often if advised.
Avoid fruit juice and fizzy drinks until diarrhoea stops.
Wash hands with soap and water; do not share towels.
Stay off school or childcare until 48 hours after the last episode.
No swimming for 2 weeks after the last episode of diarrhoea.
Shock: pale or mottled, cold extremities, weak pulses, prolonged CRT, decreased consciousness.
Clinical dehydration: low-osmolarity ORS 50 mL/kg over 4 h plus maintenance; NG tube if needed.
Initial IV maintenance: isotonic crystalloid; electrolytes and glucose at start and at least every 24 h; daily weight.
Exclusion 48 hours after the last episode; handwashing is the key control measure.

summary: You can now tell clinical dehydration from shock, plan oral rehydration and calculate maintenance fluids with Holliday-Segar. You can also choose a safe IV maintenance fluid and monitor it as NG29 requires.

A.q: Lily, 2, weighs 14 kg and has clinical dehydration without shock. Oral rehydration is prescribed. How much ORS should she have over 4 hours, in addition to maintenance?
A.why: CG84: low-osmolarity ORS 50 mL/kg over 4 hours plus maintenance. 50 x 14 = 700 mL.

whyNot.0: 350 mL is 25 mL/kg, half the recommended deficit replacement.
whyNot.1: 1,400 mL is 100 mL/kg, the IV deficit figure for a child who was shocked.
whyNot.2: 140 mL is 10 mL/kg, the size of a resuscitation bolus.

A.q: Zak weighs 16 kg and needs IV maintenance fluids after surgery. Using Holliday-Segar, what is his daily maintenance volume?
A.why: First 10 kg x 100 = 1,000 mL; next 6 kg x 50 = 300 mL; total 1,300 mL per day.

whyNot.0: 1,600 mL applies 100 mL/kg to every kilogram.
whyNot.2: 1,120 mL uses 20 mL/kg for the kilograms above 10 kg instead of 50 mL/kg.
whyNot.3: 800 mL applies 50 mL/kg to every kilogram.

A.q: Sophie, 18 months, has gastroenteritis. Which finding is a red flag sign of increased risk of shock?
A.why: Sunken eyes are one of the CG84 red flag signs, alongside appearing unwell, altered responsiveness, tachycardia, tachypnoea and reduced skin turgor.

whyNot.1: Dry mucous membranes are a sign of clinical dehydration but not a red flag.
whyNot.2: Reduced urine output is a dehydration symptom, not one of the red flags.
whyNot.3: Warm extremities are reassuring; cold extremities suggest shock.

B.q: Mia, 6, starts IV maintenance fluids on the ward. Which fluid and monitoring plan follows NICE NG29?
options: 0.18% sodium chloride with 4% glucose; electrolytes weekly
Isotonic crystalloid; electrolytes and glucose daily
0.45% sodium chloride; electrolytes if symptoms develop
B.why: NG29: initial maintenance is an isotonic crystalloid (sodium 131 to 154 mmol/L); check electrolytes and glucose at the start and at least every 24 hours, with daily weights.

whyNot.0: This is hypotonic, and weekly checks are far too infrequent.
whyNot.2: 5% glucose contains no sodium and risks severe hyponatraemia.
whyNot.3: This is hypotonic, and electrolytes must be monitored routinely, not on symptoms.

B.q: Harry, 10 months, has clinical dehydration from gastroenteritis but no red flags. He keeps refusing his oral rehydration solution. What is the next step?
options: Stop breastfeeds to rest the gut
B.why: CG84: if a child cannot drink ORS or keeps vomiting it, consider giving ORS by nasogastric tube before IV fluids.

whyNot.0: IV fluids are for shock, red flags with deterioration, or failure of ORS including by NG tube.
whyNot.1: Fruit juice should be avoided as it can worsen diarrhoea.

B.q: Ellie, 3, has gastroenteritis. Her mother asks when she can return to nursery. What advice is correct?
options: When her stools start to firm up
B.why: CG84: children should not attend school or childcare until 48 hours after the last episode of diarrhoea or vomiting.

whyNot.0: 24 hours is too short; the advice is 48 hours.
whyNot.1: Eating normally does not mean she is no longer infectious.
whyNot.2: Firmer stools do not mark the end of the exclusion period.

C.q: Noah, 18 months, weighs 11 kg. He is pale, mottled and cold, with a CRT of 5 seconds after 3 days of gastroenteritis. After the first bolus, he is still shocked. What should happen next?
C.why: CG84: if shock persists after the first rapid 10 mL/kg infusion of 0.9% sodium chloride, give a second; if it persists after that, consider intensive care.

whyNot.1: Enteral rehydration is not used while a child is shocked.
whyNot.2: Increasing maintenance does not treat circulatory failure.
whyNot.3: Waiting delays resuscitation of a shocked child.

C.q: Ben, 4, has hypernatraemic dehydration with a sodium of 158 mmol/L. How should the deficit be replaced?
options: Over 24 hours using 5% glucose as the fluid
Rapidly over 4 hours to restore volume
Over 12 hours using 0.18% sodium chloride fluid
C.why: CG84: in hypernatraemic dehydration, replace the deficit over 48 hours and keep the fall in plasma sodium below 0.5 mmol/L per hour.

whyNot.0: 24 hours is too fast and 5% glucose is hypotonic, risking cerebral oedema.
whyNot.1: Rapid correction risks cerebral oedema as water shifts into brain cells.
whyNot.3: 12 hours is too fast and a hypotonic fluid drops sodium too quickly.

C.q: Amira, 7, has meningitis and is on IV fluids. The consultant is concerned about raised antidiuretic hormone. What change to her maintenance fluid is expected?
C.why: NG29: if a child is at risk of fluid overload, for example raised ADH secretion, restrict fluids to 50 to 80% of routine maintenance.

whyNot.0: Increasing fluid with raised ADH risks fluid overload and hyponatraemia.
whyNot.1: A hypotonic fluid would worsen the risk of hyponatraemia.
whyNot.2: Stopping IV fluids is not the response; a restricted isotonic volume is.

reteach.title: Fill the tank in stages
reteach.question: If a child's fluid tank is low, what do you do first, second and third?

blocks.body: Think of three jobs. First, fix shock with a rapid 10 mL/kg bolus and reassess. Second, replace the deficit: by mouth with ORS 50 mL/kg over 4 hours where possible, or IV (50 mL/kg, or 100 mL/kg if the child was shocked). Third, keep up with ongoing needs using maintenance fluids calculated by Holliday-Segar. Monitor weight, fluid balance, electrolytes and glucose throughout.

blocks.text: A normal blood pressure does not rule out shock in a child. Children compensate with tachycardia and vasoconstriction, so hypotension is a late sign; cold peripheries, weak pulses and a prolonged CRT come first.

explain.body: Shock: decreased consciousness, pale or mottled skin, cold extremities, tachycardia, tachypnoea, weak peripheral pulses, prolonged CRT. Hypotension is a late sign in children.

test.q: Which sign suggests that a dehydrated child has progressed to shock?
test.why: Weak peripheral pulses are a sign of clinical shock in CG84.

whyNot.0: Tachycardia occurs in both dehydration and shock.
whyNot.1: Dry mucous membranes indicate dehydration, not shock.
whyNot.3: Reduced urine output is a feature of dehydration.

explain.body: Low-osmolarity ORS 50 mL/kg over 4 hours plus maintenance, given small and often. Continue breastfeeding. Use an NG tube if the child cannot drink enough or keeps vomiting.

test.q: Freddie, 2, weighs 12 kg and is clinically dehydrated. What ORS volume should he have over 4 hours plus maintenance?
test.why: 50 mL/kg x 12 kg = 600 mL over 4 hours, plus maintenance.

explain.body: Holliday-Segar: 100 mL/kg/day for the first 10 kg, 50 for the next 10 kg, 20 for each kg above 20 kg. Divide by 24 for an hourly rate.

test.q: What is the daily maintenance volume for a 30 kg child?

whyNot.0: 1,500 mL leaves out the 20 mL/kg for the kg above 20.
whyNot.2: 2,000 mL uses 50 mL/kg for the kilograms above 20 instead of 20 mL/kg.
whyNot.3: 1,900 mL adds 40 mL/kg for the kg above 20.

explain.body: Isotonic crystalloid for initial maintenance. Electrolytes and glucose at the start and at least every 24 hours; daily weight; strict fluid balance. Correct sodium by no more than 12 mmol/L in 24 hours.

test.q: How often should electrolytes be measured once a child is established on IV fluids?
options: At the end of the infusion
test.why: NG29: measure plasma electrolytes and glucose at the start and at least every 24 hours while on IV fluids.

whyNot.1: Weekly checks miss dangerous sodium changes.
whyNot.3: Monitoring must continue during the infusion, not only at the end.
